desc:
Start with an array of the same length as target in which every element is 1. Then repeat the following step as often as you like: let x be the sum of all elements currently in the array, choose any index i and set arr[i] = x.

Return true if the array can become exactly target, element by element, and false otherwise.

target = [9, 3, 5]  result = true
[1, 1, 1] -> [1, 3, 1] -> [1, 3, 5] -> [9, 3, 5]

target = [1, 1, 1, 2]  result = false
target = [8, 5]        result = true
target = [1]           result = true (nothing to do)
hints: Run the process backwards. Which element of the final array must have been written last?
The last written element is the largest one, and it equals the total of the array at that moment. Undo it: the previous value was max - (sum of the other elements).

Use a max-heap and the running total. Replace the max by max mod (sum of the others) instead of subtracting one step at a time, and reject when the others sum to 0, the result would be 0, or the others already exceed the max.
editorial: Going forward the choices are huge, but backwards the move is forced. In the last step the written element became the sum of the whole array, so it is strictly larger than every other element (for length at least 2), i.e. it is the maximum. Undo it: the old value of that cell is max - rest where rest is the sum of the other elements. If this is not at least 1 the target is impossible.

Subtracting rest one time at a time can take up to 1e9 steps, as in [1, 1000000000]. The same cell will be the maximum again and again until it drops below rest, so jump directly: the new value is max % rest. If that is 0, the cell would have to be 0 (impossible), except when rest = 1, where the cell can be reduced by 1s all the way down to 1, so the answer is true. Stop with true when the maximum is 1.

Each jump is a Euclid-style step, which at least halves the maximum, so there are O(log M) jumps per element and O(n + log M) heap operations in total. Time O(n + k log n) with k the number of jumps, memory O(n). A single-element array is true only for [1]: the rest is 0, which the loop rejects.
solution:
import heapq


def canBuildTarget(target):
    total = sum(target)
    h = [-x for x in target]
    heapq.heapify(h)
    while -h[0] > 1:
        m = -heapq.heappop(h)
        rest = total - m
        if rest == 1:
            return True
        if rest == 0 or rest >= m:
            return False
        new = m % rest
        if new == 0:
            return False
        total = rest + new
        heapq.heappush(h, -new)
    return True
